summary.text: A 67-year-old Caucasian man and ex-smoker with 43 pack-years had progressive dysphagia to solids over the last 2 years. Endoscopy, neck CT, FDG-PET and repeated biopsies at two previous hospitals raised suspicion of malignancy but did not explain the tumoral lesion. At the authors' hospital, endoscopy showed an approximately 9 cm polypoid tumor partially obstructing the esophageal lumen, with an unremarkable examination and normal laboratory data.

Because of the obstruction and concern for malignancy, he underwent successful en bloc endoscopic submucosal dissection. The 9x7x5 cm specimen showed dense lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, storiform-like fibrosis, 60 IgG4-positive plasma cells per high-power field and an IgG4/IgG ratio above 40%. Ten days after the procedure serum IgG4 was elevated at 179 mg/dL. He was diagnosed with an IgG4-related pseudotumor of the esophagus and discharged after an uneventful post-procedural course.

Two months after the procedure, neck CT showed no residual mass, but thorax CT showed a 24 mm spiculated mass in the left lower lobe, with FDG-PET hypermetabolism and mediastinal nodes. Bronchoscopy could not sample it. A left iliac crest lesion biopsy showed adenocarcinoma favoring a lung primary, and he received chemotherapy. He died 21 months after the procedure of an unknown cause, without autopsy.
